edits.target: The answer is the pivot between 'true but weaker' and 'sharper but unjustified'.
edits.content:
11. Typed rider audit (do this for the 2-3 options that survive step 4; judge each differing clause by its type, not by whether it looks stronger or safer):
   - (R1) Deviation from the stem: 'even without hypothesis H', a different set than the stem defined (a bigger set T replacing the stem's Λ), a sub-range carved out of the stem's stated range, a closed vs open endpoint. Compare the option literally with the stem. A hypothesis the stem states is there to be used, so 'even without it' is false unless you can prove it. A carved-out sub-range is a weakening of a full-range statement.
   - (R2) Conditional rider 'if H then C': check directly that H implies C, and pick the H that is exactly sufficient. Weaker properties (generically injective, finite onto its image, birational, 'at least one of the two inequalities', total mass instead of a mass function) usually do not give pointwise or global conclusions. A stronger property (separates points, injective, embedding, both inequalities) does. A rider whose hypothesis demonstrably implies its conclusion is a derivable extra and BEATS the bare option that stops before it.
   - (R3) Added structure (free factor, a basis compatible with products across all degrees, an 'iff for every parameter', a decorated object): run a cheap invariant (rank or dimension count, size of a free factor vs the ambient rank, growth rates, degenerate parameter). If you cannot make it pass, reject the option however 'strong' it looks.
   - (R4) Vague weakening of a conclusion that the same hypotheses give in sharper form ('cannot remain bounded' vs finite-time blow-up; 'a subset of X' vs X; 'some threshold' vs the explicit threshold; 'exists' vs 'equals'): reject the vague option if the sharper option passes R1-R3. Choosing the vague option needs a named failure of the sharper one, and 'it feels safer' is not a failure.
   Then rank survivors by implication and take the strongest survivor.

edits.target: ## Near-duplicate options: constants, quantifiers, ranges, exact details
edits.content: - Stem-echo check: list the objects, sets and ranges the stem names (e.g. 'for every K and every p in (-1,inf]', 'the admissible set Λ', 'n>=2'). The faithful option reuses exactly these. Options that substitute another set (T for Λ), split the range into sub-ranges with an arbitrary cut-off, exclude a point, or add 'even without the hypothesis' are altered statements. When the stem itself says 'for every X and every p in R', the answer typically quantifies over all of R. Equally, 'strongest statement for every ...' is usually an 'always can / always holds' statement on the full stated class, not an 'iff' variant defined on a bigger parameter set.

edits.target: ## Final sanity pass (do this before committing)
edits.content: Burden of proof is symmetric. If you pick the more specific option, you owe a derivation or invariant test for its extra clause (typed audit R1-R3). If you pick the plainer, vaguer or weaker option, you owe the exact extra clause of the runner-up and the concrete test it fails (a counterexample, an invariant violation, a hypothesis that does not imply the conclusion). Never justify the weaker pick by 'the other adds something I cannot fully verify' when its added clause is the standard consequence of the stated hypotheses (R2) or the sharper form of the same conclusion (R4). Never justify the stronger pick by 'it is stronger' when its added clause has no derivation (R3), deviates from the stem (R1), or contradicts a small case. Also check that the strongest-looking option does not make a claim that is false for some parameter allowed by the stem (for example n>=3 when the stem says n>=2).

edits.target: ## Trivial directions, negative hedges, iff vs one-way, FPT vs XP
edits.content:
- 'Which objects correspond / are in bijection / classify' stems: an option 'a subset of / a sub-collection of / some family inside X' is implied by the exact option 'X' and fails to identify the object, so it loses whenever the exact option survives. To test the exact option, count at the smallest parameters (e.g. one-box or rank-one case) and compare with the size of the parametrizing set; to discard variants with extra or removed conditions, check a small case where the condition would bite. Also prefer the full named object over variants that add a modification clause ('except that ... is also required to be strict', 'but do not impose condition ...') unless the count test shows the modification is needed.
- Blow-up and existence stems: with identical hypotheses on the data, 'blows up in finite time' beats 'is not globally bounded / cannot remain bounded', and 'global solution that is unbounded' is a different, usually unproved claim. Weakening the hypothesis to 'at least one of two conditions' or replacing a pointwise-in-radius condition by a total-mass condition is an inflation unless the mechanism supports it.

edits.target: ## Tie-breaker: signature of the winning option
edits.content: - Stem-diff / mirror pass (fast): write the stem's conclusion type, quantifier order, parameter range, dependence list (e.g. 'any coloring', 'all N≥2 and all β', 'constant depending on d,k,ε'), space (global vs _loc, open vs closed interval) and hypotheses, then diff each option against it for single-clause corruptions: uniqueness dropped, 'some' vs 'every', ∃ moved before ∀, endpoint added or range stretched or 'large N' substituted, hypothesis dropped ('even without'), limsup vs liminf, different norm or space, iff cut to one direction, index shifted, strictness or gap term added. The winner reproduces the stem's quantifiers and range literally and adds no rider you cannot prove, and its spaces match the regularity of the stem's data. A rival that differs from it by exactly one such edit is the distractor.

## Explicit formulas, identities and case-split options
- Options usually differ only in a sign, a swapped symbol, a permuted index slot or one shifted exponent. Do not expand everything. Diff the options symbol by symbol and test the differing slot with a degenerate specialization (a parameter = 0 or 1, a vanishing factor, a symmetry or homogeneity-degree check, a weight or count check). Keep the version that passes the test and matches the placement most options share. An isolated swap (ℓ^{N-w} vs ℓ^{N-w-1}, one lone changed range) is the single-edit corruption.
- Check internal consistency of case-split formulas: (i) each case range must contain the endpoint that the option's own definitions refer to (a sign defined by 'iff w=N' requires w=N to lie in the case that uses it); (ii) the ranges together must cover the parameter domain with no gap and no contradictory overlap.
- An option that only describes a formula in words ('a three-case formula determined by ...') is a truncation. When the stem asks for a complete classification, it loses to the option that states every case explicitly and passes the checks above.

## Negative claims: hedged tail vs sharp non-uniformity (clarification)
- Distinguish two kinds of negative content. (a) A negative TAIL attached to a positive claim ('...only', '...need not hold', 'only XP') is a downgrade hedge and is usually the corruption. (b) A BARE sharp negative that IS the theorem (e.g. 'sup over all dimensions of the norm = infinity for every r', 'no uniform bound', 'no such algorithm') can be correct, especially when the stem asks for behaviour 'uniformly over all n / all parameters' or for the strongest valid statement.
- Test for (b): every competing positive option must carry an explicit constant, rate, restricted range or threshold that you cannot derive (2n^{1/r}, C n^{1/r}/log n, 'bounded for r>2 and failing only for r≤2'). If those riders are unjustified or refuted by a simple growth or dimension count, the plain non-uniformity statement over the stem's full range wins. Do not reject it merely because it is negative, and do not choose it merely because it is the shortest option.

## Multi-property stems ('exact general validity' of two properties)
- When a stem asks for the exact validity of two related properties over all parameters, test each property separately. A correct answer often separates them (one holds unconditionally, the other iff a simple condition). Distractors merge them (both iff, or both universal), swap which property is the conditional one, or replace the clean condition with a vaguer reformulation. Never accept a 'because ...' gloss without checking that the reason actually implies the claim.
